The longest total solar eclipse on land this century promises to be the experience of a lifetime, but watching it from Luxor, Egypt, may not be straightforward. What could go wrong? Quite a lot, actually.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Aug. 2, 2027, I'll be in Luxor, Egypt, to witness what could be the greatest total solar eclipse of my life. I've seen nine total solar eclipses across the world, but this one promises to be different. For a remarkable six minutes and 22 seconds, the moon will completely cover the sun, plunging Egypt's ancient temples and monuments into eerie twilight as the solar corona bursts into view.

I've been calling it the "eclipse of the century" for many years, and for good reason. It will be the longest total solar eclipse until 2114 — and the longest on land of the 21st century — and it will take place in one of the most extraordinary places on Earth. What could go wrong?

I've chased eclipses long enough to know that the celestial mechanics are the easy part. The moon will arrive exactly on schedule — that's guaranteed. Everything else — the weather, the crowds, the transport, the equipment and the people — is rather less predictable. From the possibility of dust storms to uncertainty about whether boats will even be allowed to move on the Nile, there are plenty of reasons to be slightly wary about what awaits eclipse chasers after the ultimate bragging rights on Aug. 2, 2027. Here are the 10 things worrying me most about the 2027 total solar eclipse in Egypt.

The chances of cloud-free skies in Luxor and anywhere in Upper Egypt in August are exceptionally high — close to 100%. That's almost unheard of in eclipse-chasing. However, clouds aren't the only thing that can obscure the sun. Dust and sand are potential hazards in the Egyptian desert, and a dust storm at the wrong moment could affect—though probably not ruin—the view. Although the sun will almost certainly be visible during the eclipse, airborne dust could hide the delicate structure of the solar corona.

How many people will descend on Luxor for the eclipse? August is normally a quiet month for tourism in Luxor because of the oppressive heat. In 2027, however, the city and its surrounding urban area — population about four million — could swell as eclipse chasers, tour groups, photographers and curious visitors descend. Hotels, roads, buses and archaeological sites will all face extraordinary pressure. My biggest concern isn't necessarily the number of people watching the eclipse, but the logistical chaos it will create. Let's take Mallorca as an example for the 2026 eclipse. Authorities there had a plan for its west coast, the prime viewing region. "They were going to start closing roads from 3 p.m. on the afternoon of the eclipse," said Simon Waldram, who runs astrophotography and landscape photography workshops and who drove his tour group to the intended viewing location at 8 o'clock on the morning of the eclipse. "There were already 300 cars there, and by 11 a.m. they had shut the road." Official plans can quickly change.

Luxor in August is brutally hot. Temperatures can exceed 104 degrees Fahrenheit (40 degrees Celsius). Totality will strike at 1:02 p.m. local time (EEST). During the eclipse, from 11:40 a.m. to 2:26 p.m., the sun will be almost directly overhead. Many tour groups will stay on their hotel grounds or remain on cruise ships — relatively close to shade and air-con — though I'm also planning to keep a wet towel around my neck and carry plenty of water. However, the heat will affect the entire trip. "We're planning our visits in the early mornings and in the late afternoon, with midday just quiet time," said Khaled ElSamman, an Egyptologist at Nord Nile whose tour will witness the eclipse from a traditional dahabiya, a two-masted river boat, in Luxor. "There are reminders to drink water and keep hydrated, but it's easy to forget if you're not used to the environment and this much humidity loss."

I'll be traveling on the Nile, which sounds like a wonderfully romantic way to experience an eclipse. However, there's speculation that river traffic could be restricted, perhaps even from the previous day. "There might be a restriction on navigation on the Nile during the eclipse, so it's a bit hard to plan where we are going to watch it," said ElSamman. "We might end up in harbor, and maybe we won't be allowed to be in the middle of the water."

Even if we're safely moored in Luxor, how many other vessels will be there? The Nile looks set to be packed with cruise ships, traditional dahabiyas and smaller boats, all carrying people hoping to witness the same extraordinary event. I wonder what totality will actually look and sound like. Will there be music? Shouting? Bright lights from neighboring boats? Probably — though perhaps that's no bad thing. It's fun to experience totality in all kinds of different environments. One of my most vivid memories of the 1999 total solar eclipse in the U.K. is the atmosphere created by the people around me and the lights that came on in boats in Falmouth harbor. Perhaps the noise and excitement will become part of the magic. I just hope nobody leaves their floodlights on.

Whether eclipse chasers can bring specialist camera equipment into the country is vexing many. After all, "professional-looking" camera equipment is usually difficult to get through customs. While phones and compact cameras are fine, customs and security personnel classify large mirrorless/DSLR cameras, long telephoto lenses and heavy tripods as "professional filming gear." My reporting suggests customs officials may take a more relaxed approach to specialist camera equipment during the eclipse. However, no special customs arrangements for eclipse visitors have been confirmed. Drones are a different matter — Egypt has strict restrictions on importing and operating them, with authorization required. Bringing a drone to see this eclipse would be a mistake.

Photographing a total solar eclipse involves pointing equipment towards the sun for an extended period, using appropriate solar filters during the partial phases. In Luxor's extreme August temperatures — and with the sun almost directly overhead — overheating could become a serious issue, particularly for cameras recording video or running continuously. Eclipse chasers will need to keep equipment shaded and as cool as possible. I'll just hope to have my trusty image-stabilized binoculars with me. I bought them a decade ago specifically for total solar eclipses, and they've given me some of the most extraordinary views and moments of my life.

Watching a total solar eclipse from Karnak or another ancient Egyptian temple sounds almost impossibly romantic. But the reality could be very different. Popular archaeological sites, such as Karnak, Luxor Temple, Hatshepsut and the Valley of the Kings, could be overwhelmed by visitors. That could mean crowded entrances, long queues and limited facilities. Besides, with the eclipsed sun close to the zenith, those spectacular images of totality framed between ancient columns may be more fantasy than reality. It may be wise to avoid the crowds — and with myriad temples and ruins near Luxor, that's likely possible. "You want to make sure you're not fighting with 10,000 other tourists trying to see the same thing," said Waldram. Queueing for hours at Karnak is not the best way to enjoy one of nature's greatest events.

Every eclipse chaser who plans and books a hotel years in advance dreads the email that often arrives a few weeks before, saying a reservation has been canceled for some spurious reason. Welcome to eclipse-gouging, when hotel, lodge and Airbnb owners realize the eclipse date and hike their prices. This has already happened in Luxor, where prices have already reached about $600 per person per night for the week of the eclipse — roughly seven times higher than usual. Worse, people expect prices to keep rising as the eclipse gets closer. Owners of remaining hotels and boats are now refusing to charter or commit, waiting for higher prices. In a country where the average wage is $150-200 per month, it's understandable — a total solar eclipse is potentially a unique jackpot for many. But it makes life a little harder for eclipse chasers.

I've witnessed totality on a tennis court at sunset, standing next to a horse on a mountain and on a cruise ship in the Southern Ocean — among others — but I've never encountered the eclipsed sun almost directly overhead. I'll need to crane my neck to see it, and for a very long time. Should I lie flat on the ground? Recline on a boat deck? Or perhaps float in a swimming pool? I'm only half joking. Six minutes is a long time to stare almost vertically upward. Finding a comfortable position could make a surprisingly big difference to how much I enjoy the spectacle.

To spend six uninterrupted minutes studying the sun's ghostly corona, watching its delicate streamers stretch into space, is almost beyond comprehension. And that's why, despite all my worries, the "eclipse of the century" can't come soon enough. "It will have hiccups," said ElSamman. "But it's going to be amazing."

Jamie is an experienced science and travel journalist, stargazer and eclipse chaser who writes about exploring the night sky, solar and lunar eclipses, the Northern Lights, moon-gazing, astro-travel, astronomy and space exploration. He is the editor of WhenIsTheNextEclipse.com, author of A Stargazing Program For Beginners, co-author of The Eclipse Effect, and a senior contributor at Forbes.

#689. A material just one atom thick reveals a strange quantum secret

Scientists at the University of Osaka in Japan have made a significant discovery in quantum physics, directly observing an unusual electronic state forming where a material just one atom thick meets a metal. Known as a heavy fermion state, this phenomenon causes electrons to behave as though they have much greater mass than normal. These states are associated with extraordinary quantum effects, including unconventional superconductivity, and the discovery could provide a new way to develop materials with unusual electronic properties.

To investigate this behavior, the researchers produced a carefully controlled, single atomic layer of ytterbium and copper (YbCu2) on the surface of a copper crystal. They then used powerful synchrotron light to study the electrons and their interactions at the boundary between the two materials. The results showed that electrons confined to the thin atomic layer could interact with freely moving electrons in the copper beneath it, producing the unusual heavy fermion behavior.

The experiments uncovered two separate heavy fermion states with different characteristics. One existed primarily within the two-dimensional atomic layer, while the other reached beyond that layer and into the three-dimensional copper crystal below.

The second state was particularly important because it provided the first direct evidence of heavy fermion behavior generated by interactions across such an interface. Researchers traced the effect to the mixing, or hybridization, of localized ytterbium 4f electrons in the atomic layer with mobile conduction electrons inside the copper substrate. This interaction demonstrated how combining materials with different electronic characteristics can produce quantum behavior that neither material would necessarily exhibit on its own.

"This achievement was made possible by our continued efforts to create high-quality materials and measure their electronic states as precisely as possible," says senior author Professor Shin-ichi Kimura. "Our next goal is to engineer and control such heavy-electron states, opening the way to previously unexplored quantum states, including unconventional superconductivity."

A New Approach to Designing Quantum Materials

The discovery suggests that the boundaries between materials could become powerful tools for creating and controlling exotic quantum states. Rather than relying only on the properties of individual substances, scientists may be able to develop entirely new electronic behaviors by carefully selecting and combining ultrathin atomic layers with suitable underlying materials.

Future research could focus on adjusting the structures of these interfaces, controlling the electronic orbitals involved, and manipulating moiré patterns that arise when atomic arrangements overlap. Such approaches may allow researchers to produce and fine-tune quantum phenomena in materials with extremely small dimensions, including effects that cannot be achieved in conventional materials. Ultimately, this could open new possibilities for engineering advanced quantum materials and investigating unconventional superconductivity.

#688. U2 Wind Back the Years With Classics, Dolly Parton Tribute for Thanksgiving Eve NFL Halftime Show

The Rock Hall-inducted group headlined the halftime show, which streamed live late Wednesday, Nov. 25 on Netflix.

The legendary Irish rock band, as they’ve done so often in the past, stepped into the cauldron, rocked out, and gave everyone what they were looking for.

On this occasion, Bono, The Edge, Adam Clayton and Larry Mullen Jr. stepped into the colosseum that is the NFL‘s first-ever Thanksgiving Eve game at SoFi Stadium, pitting the Los Angeles Rams against the visiting Green Bay Packers. Explore Bono U2 See latest videos, charts and news

The Rock Hall-inducted group headlined the halftime show, which streamed live late Wednesday, Nov. 25 on Netflix. At the very top, the four bandmates took the long walk to the centerfield as a choir recited the lyrics of “I Still Haven’t Found What I’m Looking For.”

“Thank you for having us,” Bono remarked over Mullen’s iconic, military-style drum pattern that launched the mini-set proper with “Sunday Bloody Sunday,” one of the band’s early political anthems. The production stepped up several gears as a marching band assembled and the song shapeshifted, interpolating The Supremes’ “Stop! In The Name of Love.”

Then, a change in mood as U2 paid tribute to Dolly Parton, the late queen of country’s smiling image splashed on three sails towering over the circular, center stage. Bono dueted with Dolly’s vocals for “Torn,” her very last recording which appears on the band’s 16th and latest studio album, Carnaval de Luz.

And, in a moment that earned a roar from the audience, the band slotted seamlessly into another Joshua Tree number, “Where The Streets Have No Name.” The sails came down, and U2 got down to rockstar business — with some support from scores of backing singers.

Without missing a beat, Bono and Co. reached into their glorybox with a rendition of “Pride (In The Name of Love)” a tribute to the assassinated civil rights leader Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., which appeared on their 1984 LP The Unforgettable Fire. And with that, U2 was done and it was game on.

Carnaval de Luz this month debuted at No. 1 on three Billboard charts, including No. 1 on Top Rock Albums, Vinyl Albums and Indie Store Album Sales, and became the band’s 14th top 10 on the Billboard 200 (opening at No. 4). It’s their 12th No. 1 on the Official U.K. Albums Chart and Australia’s ARIA Chart.

U2 this year chalks up its 50th anniversary, the celebrations for which will accelerate next year when the band returns to stadiums around the globe with Carnaval De Luz presents: The Greatest Show on Earth, its first stadium tour since 2019. Watch highlights from the Thanksgiving Eve halftime show and check out the setlist below. Stream the full performance here on Netflix.

#687. How AI is likely to change Germany's job market

The scale of the economic disruption caused by AI has led even conservative politicians to talk about universal basic income. But economists aren't convinced, and campaigners think we need to ask deeper questions.

At the German government's 2026 Digital Summit in early November, Chancellor Friedrich Merz was asked by a journalist to square a difficult economic circle: If artificial intelligence could make hundreds of thousands of people redundant in the next few years, might it become necessary for the government to give people a basic income to ease the ensuing economic disaster?

Surprisingly, Merz didn't respond with a flat dismissal — as might be expected from a conservative politician known for his neoliberal, market-friendly views.

"I've always been a bit cautious about this issue in recent years," he said, as reported by the news outlet RND. "However, I'm also well aware that the issue of AI will change our working world so fundamentally that we'll have to give serious thought to many of these issues in the coming years — including the question: Is our productivity not good enough?"

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What makes this ambiguity notable is that much of Merz's policies since becoming chancellor last year have involved making Germans work more: His government's planned pension reforms would see Germany's retirement age being raised. In July, he announced a crackdown on sick leave. And in spring 2025, having barely taken office, he caused much consternation by criticizing the concept of a "work-life balance" and declaring, "We in this country must work more and more efficiently."

But those policies seem to contradict the impending realities of the labor market in an AI world.

This week, the head of Germany's Federal Employment Agency, Andrea Nahles, warned that the introduction AI would cost Germany as many 800,000 jobs in the next 15 years. Though she also said AI could eventually create a similar number of jobs, clearly the socioeconomic upheaval would be considerable.

Nahles is not the only leading figure concerned about job losses caused by AI. Karsten Wildberger, Germany's minister for digital transformation and government modernization, takes any opportunity he can to warn that Germany must prepare for the economic disruptions of AI.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

And even for Wildberger, a former CEO of a massive retail company, part of the future economy might come down to giving people free money. He was convinced, he told the Neue Osnabrücker Zeitung in March, "that an unconditional basic income can be part of the solution to cushion the upheavals in the labor market."

Campaigners have cautiously welcomed this new openness from unexpected quarters. "It shows that in the face of technological transformation we also need to look differently at the question of how we need to secure people's economic stability," said Kirsten Herrmann, board member at the nonprofit Mein Grundeinkommen (My Basic Income), which runs various projects examining the social and economic impact of universal basic income (UBI).

"But I also think that individual statements by politicians don't amount to a political change, of course," she told DW. "It just means that we need to enter a serious and constructive debate about what kind of a role a basic income can play."

The idea of a universal basic income is very old: English Renaissance philosopher Thomas More mentions it in his 1516 book Utopia, for instance. But since the 20th century, it has largely been seen as an idealistic notion adopted by leftists — that is, until some of the world's most high-profile tech bosses latched onto the idea as a way to offset the utopian advances they said AI would bring.

In 2017, Elon Musk, who had co-founded the corporation OpenAI two years earlier, predicted that a universal basic income would at some stage become inevitable. Since then, leading figures in the AI sector, including Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, and Sam Altman, the other founder of OpenAI, have all gone on record in support of UBI (though Altman's interest has cooled somewhat since he launched a massive UBI experiment in the US in 2019).

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

But Herrmann said it's a "double-edged sword" when such figures mention the idea. She isn't convinced that organizations like hers and people Elon Musk want the same thing.

"On the one hand, it's always nice when the debate about a basic income gets attention from prominent voices," she said. "On the other hand, the basic income that people from the tech business talk about is a kind of neoliberal basic income: They talk about what to do when there are no more profitable jobs for people, because they still actually do need people to do certain things, whereas we talk about a basic income that is meant to give people a secure economic base — before the crisis in the job market happens."

What makes the comments of Merz and Wildberger all the more eyebrow-raising is that mainstream German economists have long since rejected the basic income idea.

Dominik Enste, director of the democracy, society, and economic ethics department at the German Economic Institute in Cologne, dismissed the idea out of hand — AI or no AI. UBI was, he said, just too expensive, especially in a country that already has plenty of social welfare costs.

"Many economists have calculated that implementing this in many countries is financially unfeasible — in Germany, for one, simply because of the need to fund commitments that have already been made (including pension payments)," he told DW in an email.

However, he also added: "We will have to change our social security systems if work is replaced by AI and, if necessary, tax AI-generated income. But it will be a conditional basic income that still provides incentives to earn a living."

Other economists are more positive about the idea. "How this plays out depends on many choices we make, and on who makes these choices, in whose interest," said Maximilian Kasy, professor of economics at the University of Oxford and author of a book on the impact of AI on society. "But a lot of the current thrust is to replace workers to increase profits and increase corporate control, though this is not the only path possible."

Kasy thinks a basic income could be a good solution, "especially if it's financed in a progressive way (so that only those at the lower end of the income distribution are net recipients)," he wrote. "The 'small print' matters very much, though!"

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

If the warnings of Wildberger, Musk, Altman et al. are to be believed, AI is already causing a bigger upheaval than any other technological advance in history, partly because of the speed of the innovations, but also because of the scale of the potential impact.

AI innovation is affecting the jobs of the traditional urban middle classes across the entire world. In 2024, the International Monetary Fund predicted that some 40% of employment in the world would be shaped by AI innovations, and as much as 60% in rich, industrialized nations.

For her part, Herrmann thinks we are not yet asking the truly fundamental questions about the socioeconomic implications of AI: Not just how do we replace the lost jobs and keep the capitalist system going, but what do we actually want to use AI for? As she put it: "Who actually profits when we become more productive through AI? And how do we redistribute that profit to everyone?"

This, she argued, is why there needs to be more debate about how exactly AI is used in the world of work. "Which jobs are going to be replaced by AI is not some law of nature," said Herrmann . "It's something that we can shape politically and socially — and then the bigger question is: Who gets a say?"

#686. Scientists tracked kids for 8 years. What they found about screen time was surprising

An eight-year study of children in Finland has revealed a surprising connection between screen time and brain function. Researchers found that children who spent more time using screens tended to have better cognitive processing abilities as teenagers, challenging the widespread assumption that screen time is necessarily harmful to developing brains.

The findings suggest that the amount of time children spend in front of screens may be less important than how they use that time. Activities that encourage learning, creativity, and problem-solving could be particularly valuable. Researchers emphasize that the goal should not be to eliminate screen time, but to balance it with physical activity and mentally stimulating experiences.

The discovery comes amid growing concerns about insufficient physical activity among teenagers. A sedentary lifestyle has been linked to poorer academic performance, while regular exercise is known to support brain function, particularly in adults. However, scientists still have much to learn about how physical activity, sitting, and screen use during childhood influence thinking abilities later in adolescence.

These questions are especially important because childhood and adolescence are critical periods of brain development. Changes in attention, memory, and learning during these years can have lasting consequences, potentially influencing educational opportunities and career paths well into adulthood.

To investigate these relationships, Finnish researchers examined how screen time, physical activity, and sedentary behavior from childhood through adolescence were associated with cognitive performance in teenagers. They also explored whether the connections differed between boys and girls and whether the intensity of physical activity made a difference.

More Screen Time Linked to Better Thinking Skills

One of the study's most unexpected findings was that greater screen time throughout childhood was associated with better cognitive processing in adolescence.

Cognitive processing refers to the mental abilities people use to take in information, pay attention, remember details, learn new things, and solve problems. These abilities play an important role in school performance and everyday decision-making.

The findings challenge the idea that all screen time should be viewed as harmful. However, the researchers caution that the relationship may depend on what children are actually doing while using digital devices. Watching videos, playing games that require strategic thinking, and engaging in educational activities may involve very different levels of mental effort.

"The findings suggest that screen time can support children's and adolescents' cognitive processing. Presumably, the essential point here is what kind of things they do in their screen time. Teachers and parents should encourage children to use devices and screens in such ways that promote active thinking, problem-solving, creativity, and learning," states Doctoral Researcher Petri Jalanko from the University of Jyväskylä.

"We should not regard screen time solely as harmful but seek balance between physical activity and screen time that promotes active thinking," Jalanko summarizes.

Exercise Affects Boys' and Girls' Brains Differently

The researchers also uncovered a more complicated picture of how physical activity relates to thinking and memory.

Among girls, spending more time engaged in light-intensity physical activity since childhood was associated with better working memory during adolescence. For boys, greater participation in guided physical activity over the same period was linked to stronger working memory.

Working memory is the brain's ability to temporarily hold and use information. It allows someone to remember instructions while completing a task, keep track of numbers during mental calculations, or follow a conversation while processing new information.

Light-intensity physical activity generally includes relatively gentle movements that do not substantially increase breathing or heart rate. Guided physical activity refers to exercise carried out with some form of instruction or supervision, such as organized sports or structured exercise sessions.

The differences between boys and girls suggest that the relationship between exercise and brain health may depend on more than simply how much a person moves. The type of activity, how it is organized, and the individual's sex could all play a role.

Another Surprising Finding About Physical Activity

The study produced another counterintuitive result. Teenagers who reported spending less time in unsupervised physical activity tended to perform better on measures of cognitive processing.

Yet when researchers used wearable sensors to objectively measure movement and heart rate, they found no association between overall physical activity or sedentary time and cognitive performance.

One possible explanation is that wearable devices measure movement without revealing what a person is actually doing. For example, a sensor may record periods of sitting or physical activity, but it cannot determine whether someone is solving a difficult problem, studying, participating in an organized activity, or simply resting.

This distinction could help explain why questionnaire responses revealed relationships that were not apparent in the sensor measurements.

"Our study indicates that the connections of physical activity and sedentary behavior to cognitive processing are complex and depend on the sex, the type and assessment method of physical activity and sedentary time. Moreover, boys and girls may benefit from different types of physical activity in view of brain health," Jalanko adds.

"However, we need more intervention studies to find out causal relations and sex differences in this respect. Moreover, it is important to examine more specifically the effects of the intensity of physical activity on changes taking place in cognitive processing."

The findings come from an eight-year follow-up conducted as part of the PANIC study, a long-running Finnish research project investigating children's physical activity and nutrition.

The current analysis included 260 participants, consisting of 124 girls and 136 boys. Their average age at the adolescent assessment was 15.8 years.

Researchers collected information about physical activity and sedentary behavior using both questionnaires and wearable devices that combined heart rate monitoring with movement measurements. This approach allowed them to compare participants' reported activities with data collected by sensors.

To evaluate cognitive abilities, the researchers used the CogState test battery, a collection of computerized assessments designed to measure aspects of mental performance. The tests examined learning, attention, and working memory.

Importantly, the findings show associations rather than cause and effect. They do not establish that increasing screen time will improve a child's thinking abilities or that reducing certain types of exercise will produce cognitive benefits. Intervention studies, in which researchers deliberately change participants' activities and measure the results, are needed to determine whether these relationships are causal.

Nevertheless, the results offer an important perspective on the continuing debate over children's screen use. Rather than treating all time spent with digital devices as equally harmful, the researchers suggest paying closer attention to whether those activities encourage active thinking and learning.

The research also highlights the importance of considering different forms of physical activity rather than focusing exclusively on the total amount of exercise children receive.

Together, the findings suggest that supporting healthy brain development may require a more nuanced approach, one that combines physical activity with opportunities for learning, creativity, and mental engagement, including those that take place on screens.

The study was published in the scientific journal Pediatric Exercise Science.

#685. Andy Taylor Was Full of Surprises: Six Deep-Dive Career Moments

Following his death at the age of 65, Billboard has highlighted some impressive, but overlooked moments from Andy Taylor's Hall of Fame career.

Andy Taylor, the founding guitarist with Duran Duran, who passed away Monday (Nov. 23) following a years-long battle with prostate cancer, aged 65, just might be the most underrated musician to emerge from the early 1980s.

Taylor, who would also form The Power Station, enjoyed a solo career and was something of a serial collaborator, stood tall in a golden era for electric guitarists. Even the slickest commercial pop songs had destructive guitar solos, the type of which seem to be lost to this generation and last.

Forget the Cold War, there was another arms race where the weapons of choice were plugged-in six-strings, with rows of effects pedals. Eddie Van Halen, Steve Vai, Joe Satriani, The Edge, Steve Stevens, Yngwie Malmsteen, Steve Lukather. It was an expansive group, and Andy Taylor was a member.

Born in Tynemouth and raised in Cullercoats, Northumberland, in north east England, Taylor was the wild boy in Duran Duran – his autobiography from 2008 even carried that title.

Here was a roguish rockstar with fast hands, itchy feet, who didn’t follow trends, but had many, many followers. But because of his breakthrough with Duran Duran, a band that drew a mystifying flood of hate from critics of the time, Taylor’s talents were largely overlooked.

Duran Duran split into two camps following the release of the 1985 James Bond hit “A View To A Kill.” Andy and John Taylor formed The Power Station, the funk-rock supergroup with Robert Palmer at the front, and Tony Thompson at the back, while Simon Le Bon, Nick Rhodes and Roger Taylor launched Arcadia, a collaborative-stacked project that, in an alternative universe, would’ve been Duran Duran’s fourth studio album.

With The Power Station, Andy Taylor was unleashed. We got shredding, finger tapping, the works. Taylor contributed to the Duran Duran album from 1986, Notorious, then he was out. Fifteen years later, he returned to the band with original drummer Roger Taylor, to reunite the Fab Five. He contributed to the 2004 album Astronaut, and again on the 2023 collection Danse Macabre.

The music world learned of his illness when, in 2022, Duran Duran was inducted into the Rock And Roll Hall of Fame. Taylor, his bandmates explained, as they read out a letter from the guitarist, was unable to attend due to illness.

Billboard has compiled six deep-dive moments from Andy Taylor’s Hall of Fame career.

In 1984, Duran Duran was on top of the world. The previous year, the band dropped Seven And The Ragged Tiger, their first U.K. No. 1 album. Its opening track, “The Reflex,” gave them a first No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100. The following year, in 1985, another U.S. No. 1 with “A View To A Kill.” A 1984 tour documentary, Sing Blue Silver, a line from the fan favorite Rio album closer “The Chauffeur,” captured the band on the road, but also gave Duranies an unexpected smack to the funnybone. Andy Taylor has one of the standout moments when he ignited an impromptu, running double-entendre joke at a press conference, a response to a question on when he learned to play his instrument. The punchline is a knockout.

With The Power Station, Andy Taylor was off the leash. The first single, “Some Like It Hot,” showcased his mad skills. With their cover of T-Rex’s “Get It On (Bang a Gong),” he was on fire. Perhaps his finest work is on “Murderess,” which the band performed at the Philadelphia leg of Live Aid in 1985, with Michael Des Barres slotting in on vocal duties when Robert Palmer dropped out. With Des Barres on board, the fourpiece made an appearance on Miami Vice. Check out the studio cut and the live version of “Murderess” below.

During the 1985 recording sessions for The Power Station’s self-titled debut album at the Power Station studio in New York City, Taylor recorded his tasty licks and explosive solos in the control room rather than out in the main live room. The reason behind it was to create an almost-live atmosphere, with producer Bernard Edwards part of his audience. Watch from 3.40 in this behind the scenes footage. “A lead guitarist, their personalities are usually fire,” the late Chic great Edwards explains. “It’s usually pretty hot. And he is a lead guitarist.”

After splitting with Duran Duran, and moving on from The Power Station (he would contribute to a second album, Living In Fear, released in 1996), Taylor took the natural next step and started a solo career. For the entre, he presented “Take It Easy,” which appeared on the soundtrack for the 1986 feature film American Anthem. It was as different to a Duran Duran song as one could imagine. And Andy, for the first time, was on vocal duties. A full solo album, Thunder, followed in 1987.

Andy Taylor was constantly on the move, recording with Robert Palmer (he played the guitar parts on his 1986 hit “Addicted to Love”), and with the likes of Rod Stewart, the Almighty, Love and Money, Tina Arena, Then Jerico and Belinda Carlisle.

“I was blessed to work with Andy Taylor – such a genius… he played the guitar solo in MAD ABOUT YOU, appears in the video and he made special appearances onstage for some of my first solo shows. What a talent,” writes Carlisle on social media. “Thank you Andy Taylor for the music and all of the joy you brought to the world which will live on forever. I hope you are feeling the love…Godspeed.”

Taylor appears in the official music video at the 2.07 mark.

In the 1980s, Andy operated Rio’s (also known as Rio Bar), a wine bar and restaurant in Whitley Bay, England. It was, of course, named after the band’s hit sophomore album and its title track. In 1985, a vandal reportedly smashed the venue’s piranha tank, spilling hundreds of gallons of water and letting loose its carnivorous occupants. It’s not known what happened with the fish, but the spot ultimately changed hands.

STS-33 was the fifth mission dedicated to the Department of Defense.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Nov. 22, 1989, the space shuttle Discovery launched on the secret mission STS-33 for the U.S. military. It lifted off from Kennedy Space Center and up into the dark of night.

This was the third nighttime launch of the shuttle program and the 32nd shuttle mission overall. Discovery had five astronauts on board. Their mission was to deploy a classified payload for the U.S. Department of Defense. NASA and the military launched several secretive shuttle missions to deploy military satellites.

The satellite that launched with STS-33 is believed to be a type of spy satellite called Magnum. But exactly what Magnum was doing in orbit remains classified.

From its start, the Space Transportation System, better known as the space shuttle, was a compromise between meeting civilian and military needs. NASA saw the vehicle as a means of supporting science research, establishing an on-orbit economy (servicing commercial satellites and flying company payloads) and ultimately, assembling the parts for a space station.

The Department of Defense saw the shuttle as an asset to deploying and retrieving reconnaissance satellites, among other projects, some of them classified. It was not until the loss of the space shuttle Challenger, that it was decided that the shuttle would only be used by the military when it was key to national security. Other needs would be met by expendable launch vehicles (ELVs).As an aside, the STS-33 astronauts also spent Thanksgiving in space during this mission. But the holiday was off to a crappy start when the shuttle's toilet broke first thing in the morning. After spending most of the day fixing it, they got to enjoy their Thanksgiving turkey together.

Hanneke joined the Space.com team in 2016 as a staff writer and producer, covering topics including spaceflight and astronomy. She currently lives in Seattle, home of the Space Needle, with her cat and two snakes. #683. Can Beijing scale up its smart-city ambitions?

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Hepeng Jia is a freelance science writer based in Suzhou, China.

Yizhuang, the district of Beijing where this Lingyi iTech robotics factory is located, is a key area of the city for demonstrating leading smart-city solutions.Credit: Qilai Shen/Bloomberg via Getty Images

In Yizhuang, a high-tech industrial zone in Beijing, drivers have access to parts of roads, highways and intersections where they might experience green lights all the way. Networks of road cameras and sensors feed data to a local control centre, which issues app notifications to drivers about upcoming interruptions, recommended driving speeds and lane suggestions to keep the traffic moving. On these ‘green-wave corridors’, the average number of traffic stops throughout the day has dropped by 40.6%, and the average travel speed has increased by 15.1%, according to local reports.

Also known as the Beijing Economic-Technological Development Area, or Beijing E-Town, Yizhuang was created in the early 1990s by the Beijing Municipal People’s Government to act as the city’s leading smart-city demonstration zone. Alongside its intelligent transport systems, it has become a key area for autonomous-vehicle development and robotics, often showcasing emerging technologies at public events.

The annual Beijing E-Town Half-Marathon, for example, attracts hundreds of humanoid robots built by companies and university teams to compete with humans over an almost 22-kilometre track. In 2025, the inaugural year of the race, many robots failed to finish. But in this year’s race, held in April, the robots showed major improvements in speed, reliability and autonomy.

Alongside Yizhuang, Beijing has many other smart-city ‘brains’ — hubs of innovation that are fast-tracking technological development in strategic areas such as artificial intelligence, digital infrastructure and data governance.

One such area is Haidian in northwest Beijing, which runs a spatial-mapping platform that functions as a digital twin of the district. Gathering data from some 170,000 buildings, plus tens of thousands of road cameras and sensors, the platform flags local faults and automatically generates work orders to speed up repairs. The repair-response time for missing manhole covers, for instance, which is a major hazard for drivers and pedestrians, has been reduced from a whole day to just four hours. Haidian is home to Peking University and Tsinghua University — two of China’s leading academic institutions in the Nature Index — as well as the country’s greatest concentration of Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) institutes.

Underpinning Beijing’s smart-city ambitions is its enormous investment in science and technology. Beijing has been the leading science city in the Nature Index since 2016, and in 2025, its Share in the natural and health sciences was about two-thirds higher than that of its closest competitor, Shanghai. That year, Beijing spent around 6% of its gross domestic product on R&D — the highest share in the country. The city’s sprawling research system has formed close ties with its private AI sector, which, as of 2024, encompassed about 2,400 companies worth nearly 350 billion yuan (US$51.7 billion).

A key challenge for Beijing is how to link all of the data being collected by its various districts and zones. Different departments might not feel incentivized to share their data or link up with central databases, says Yuan Zhibin, a senior research fellow at the CAS Institute of Science and Technology Strategy Consulting in Beijing. Strong competition between Beijing’s leading technology districts, such as Yizhuang and Haidian, as well as the costs involved in changing or updating systems, are major factors, says Yuan.

#682. Autistic brains look surprisingly similar on average. Then scientists looked closer.

Brain scans have revealed a surprising pattern in people with autism. Although adults with and without autism showed remarkably similar brain activity when researchers compared group averages, a closer examination uncovered striking differences between individuals. These differences were especially pronounced in brain regions involved in understanding and responding to social information.

The findings, published in JNeurosci, suggest that looking at average brain activity may conceal important differences among people with autism spectrum disorder (ASD). The discovery could help scientists better understand why autism varies so widely from person to person and eventually support more personalized approaches to care.

The research was led by Dorit Kliemann and James Traer of the University of Iowa, who worked with collaborators to investigate how brain activity differs between adults with and without autism.

What Brain Scans Reveal When People Watch Movies

To explore these differences, the team examined previously collected brain imaging data from Indiana University and Caltech. The recordings captured brain activity as adults with and without autism watched movies from several genres, including animation, action, romantic comedy, and Hitchcockian thrillers.

Movies offered researchers a way to study how the brain responds to a constantly changing stream of sights, sounds, and social interactions. Unlike simple laboratory tasks, movies present a rich mixture of information that more closely resembles the complexity of everyday experiences.

Using the imaging data, the researchers trained a computational model to identify connections between brain activity and different elements of the movies. These included visual details, sounds, and more abstract social information, such as interactions between characters.

After training, the model was able to accurately predict activity across several brain systems.

Kliemann explained why this approach is particularly useful for investigating the social challenges sometimes associated with autism: "The computational model allowed us to look for robust brain responses to many different aspects of the complex, dynamic contexts in the movies."

A Surprising Difference Hidden by Brain Activity Averages

The most unexpected finding emerged when researchers compared the two groups.

At first, the results suggested relatively little difference. When brain responses were averaged across participants, the model predicted activity in various brain systems similarly for adults with and without autism.

However, the picture changed when the researchers examined how much individual participants differed from others in their own group.

People with autism showed substantially greater variation in their brain responses than participants without autism. In other words, although the overall group averages looked similar, the responses of individual autistic participants were much less alike.

This increased variability appeared across nearly every brain system examined. The strongest differences occurred in the social brain system, a network of regions involved in processing social information and understanding other people.

Why the Findings Could Change Autism Research

The results raise important questions about how scientists investigate autism. Many existing approaches to understanding and treating the condition rely heavily on comparing average measurements from groups of autistic and nonautistic individuals.

But if autistic people show considerable differences in how their brains process information, these averages may obscure some of the most meaningful findings.

Traer described the team's surprise: "We were surprised by the similarity of group averages. The results suggest that we need to focus on understanding the details of individual brain responses. How and why do they differ?"

Rather than searching only for brain activity patterns shared by everyone with autism, the findings point toward the potential value of studying individuals and identifying smaller groups with similar characteristics.

Kliemann highlighted what this could mean for future research and support: "Identifying ASD subgroups may help us build a more precise understanding of the condition and help develop ways to provide individually tailored support."

The researchers now plan to investigate how these differences in brain activity relate to variations in autism-related behavior. They hope to determine where and when the differences emerge, how they are connected to individual characteristics, and what might explain them.

Ultimately, the findings suggest that understanding autism may require looking beyond the average brain and paying closer attention to the distinctive ways individuals process the world.

#681. The hidden language of psychopathy is not what scientists expected

The way people describe their lives may offer surprising clues about their personalities, including traits associated with psychopathy. A new study from the University of Mississippi challenges the familiar image of psychopaths as cold and emotionless, revealing that their patterns of language can be far more complex than expected.

Researchers examined hundreds of personal life stories and discovered that three major traits associated with psychopathy, boldness, meanness, and disinhibition, were connected to distinctly different ways of using words. Some of the findings were particularly unexpected. For example, people who scored higher in meanness tended to use more positive language, while those with greater boldness used fewer words associated with anxiety.

The findings, published in the journal Personality and Individual Differences, suggest that psychopathic traits can influence everyday communication in subtle ways that conventional stereotypes often overlook.

"The goal here is not to diagnose psychopathy based on language," said Ky Bray, an Ole Miss doctoral candidate in psychology. "It's to point to the fact that psychopathy shows up in everyday behaviors, even subtle behaviors like language.

"If we want to understand psychopathy and the different traits that comprise it, we need to think creatively about how these traits shape social interaction."

What 450 Life Stories Revealed About Psychopathy

The researchers used a psychological framework known as the Triarchic Model of Psychopathy, which examines three distinct personality dimensions. Boldness generally involves confidence and fearlessness, meanness reflects tendencies toward callousness and reduced empathy, and disinhibition involves difficulties with impulse control. According to Laura Drislane, an assistant professor of psychology at the University of Mississippi, these characteristics can affect ordinary behaviors, including how people describe their own experiences.

To investigate these connections, Drislane and Bray recruited 450 participants, including college students and individuals who reported having been incarcerated. Each person responded to open questions about important moments in their life, including their greatest highs, lowest points, and major turning points.

After writing their personal accounts, participants completed a questionnaire designed to measure their levels of psychopathic traits. The researchers then analyzed the written responses using specialized software that identifies patterns in word choice.

The analysis focused on how frequently participants used language associated with different psychological categories, including positive and negative emotions, achievement, social influence or clout, and risk. By comparing these language patterns with the personality scores, the team identified several intriguing relationships.

Surprising Differences in Positive and Negative Language

Participants with higher disinhibition scores generally used more negative words in their personal stories. They were also less likely to mention friends or use language connected to positive emotions and personal achievement.

Meanness, however, showed a very different pattern. People scoring higher in this trait tended to use more positive language, along with more words related to achievement and rewards. They also used fewer expressions associated with negative emotions.

Boldness was associated with another distinctive pattern. Participants with higher scores used fewer anxiety-related words, including terms such as fear, afraid, and worry. Their personal accounts also contained fewer references to mental illness.

These differences suggest that psychopathic traits do not produce a single recognizable style of communication. Instead, different characteristics are associated with different ways of describing emotions, goals, relationships, and personal experiences.

"What this tells us is the story we tell about our life has meaning," Drislane said. "It helps people make sense of their experiences, develop a worldview and a coherent sense of who they are.

"What we're starting to see is that in psychopathy, there are traits that relate to differences in meaning-making and the ways people think about their life."

Why Psychopathy Is More Complex Than the Stereotypes

The researchers also discovered that the relationship between personality traits and language changed depending on which question participants were answering. Someone describing a difficult experience, for example, might use language differently than when recalling a personal success.

This variation is important because it challenges the assumption that psychopathy is characterized by consistently flat or emotionally empty communication. Instead, the findings indicate that language patterns depend on both the particular psychopathic trait and the context in which someone is telling their story.

"People tend to think of psychopathy as one thing, but it's actually multidimensional," Bray said. "What we mean when we say that everyone exists on this spectrum. Everyone has some degree of meanness, boldness, and disinhibition.

"Viewing it from a multidimensional perspective allows us to observe how those traits might manifest in nonforensic populations, in people who have not committed a crime. That allows us to see how these traits affect college students, business professionals, or interpersonal relationships."

Like many personality conditions, psychopathy is better understood as a spectrum rather than a simple distinction between people who have it and those who do not. At one extreme is the familiar cultural image of a "psychopath," while people at the opposite end score low in all three dimensions.

This approach allows researchers to examine psychopathic traits throughout the general population, including among people who have never committed a crime. It also helps explain why the same broad label can encompass individuals with very different personalities and behaviors.

How Understanding Psychopathic Traits Could Improve Treatment

Recognizing these differences has implications beyond understanding everyday speech. Researchers have linked dimensions of psychopathy to serious outcomes, including criminal behavior, repeat offending, and intimate partner violence. Examining each trait separately may provide a clearer picture of how these risks develop.

"That's in part why there's a movement away from calling people 'psychopaths,' because we don't view psychopathy as a category," Drislane said. "But psychopathic dimensions can predict important outcomes, things like crime, recidivism, or intimate partner violence.

"What our research, including this paper, suggests is that it's important to look beyond that label and into the different components or dimensions of psychopathy, because each of those dimensions actually has a unique set of outcomes or things that it can predict."

Researchers also emphasize that psychopathy can be treated, with interventions aimed at reducing problematic symptoms and behaviors. Understanding the psychological processes behind boldness, meanness, and disinhibition could help scientists develop more targeted approaches and potentially identify ways to prevent severe problems from emerging.

"If we want to be able to treat or ideally even prevent psychopathy from developing, we need to understand the mechanisms at play," she said. "That comes down to understanding the unique contributors for all three of these dimensions."

Materials provided by University of Mississippi. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

"Star Trek: First Contact" celebrates its 30th anniversary today, and the engaging sci-fi classic still looks fantastic three decades later. With the sad passing of its star, Patrick Stewart, last month, and "Star Trek's" milestone 60th birthday taking place in 2026, this is a bittersweet salute that also holds an extra special significance.

Directed by "The Next Generation's" Number One, Jonathan Frakes, in his feature film debut, "First Contact" consistently ranks as one of the finest "Star Trek" feature films among fans and critics, and those accolades are well deserved.

Based on a compelling screenplay by Brannon Braga and Ronald D. Moore, "First Contact" remains as bright and beautiful as ever, brimming with bravado, heart, horror, and heroism.

Not only was it a bona fide crowdpleaser when it was released by Paramount over Thanksgiving week on Nov. 22, 1996, but it was also a financial success for the studio, eventually pulling in a worldwide total of $212 million off a modest $45 million budget.

Honestly, who can forget Alice Krige's seductive Borg Queen, Marina Sirtis’ Deana Troi tipsy on tequila, Brent Spiner's Data feeling the sensation of human skin, Patrick Stewart’s Jean-Luc Picard reliving past traumas, and James Cromwell's Zephram Cochrane blasting off in the Phoenix and dancing to Roy Orbison's "Ooby Dooby"?

We caught up with Frakes for "First Contact's" 30th anniversary to hear why this "Trek" treasure holds up and warp back to Hollywood’s heyday of the '90s. Resistance is futile!

"What’s not to love?" Frakes tells SPACE regarding the film’s lasting popularity. "It was bulletproof. Dean Devlin ["Stargate," "Independence Day"] and I have very similar sensibilities about filmmaking. We like the whole idea of action, adventure, comedy, and in the case of 'First Contact,' a little horror as well. ILM’s John Knoll, the guy who won the Oscar for 'Star Wars,' just happened to be our Special Effects Supervisor."

"First Contact" is filled with memorable moments and indelible performances, some of which certainly stand out for Frakes looking back over the years on the production.

"The two things that always come to mind were the beautiful scene with Alfre [Woodard] and Patrick, the Moby Dick scene, where she says, 'You broke your little ships,'" he recalls. "I was sitting under the camera with my face in my hands, watching two heavyweights go at it take after take. It was what you dream of. They were into it. The writing was great. We had time to do it right, and they were fabulous together.

"That and the Cromwell and Marina drunk on tequila scene. It's not only one extended take, but it contributes to the pace of the movie in the right kind of way. My wife tells me that I was really good in that scene because I was exhausted and relaxed. It’s true, you’re exhausted when you’re filming and acting at the same time. I got to sit there and watch those two. It was like watching a tennis game."

Many Trekkies might not know that Alfre Woodard is Frakes' godmother, and he had specifically asked producer Rick Berman for approval to include her in the movie’s cast.

"She's one of our finest American actors," he notes. "Rick said, 'If we can get Alfre, that would be great.' I knew she’d do great with Patrick, so that was a no-brainer. I never had a godmother, and when I came out here to live in LA back in 1979, an old friend from college, Nathan Cook, was working with Alfre. We were at a barbecue, and it came up. She said, 'You don’t have a godmother? I’ll be your godmother.' I asked what that meant, and she said, 'I’ll be in charge of your spiritual being.' It's been a magical friendship that turned into her playing that part."

The hive-minded cybernetic collective known as the Borg featured prominently in the time-travel tale, and that second filming unit did a masterful job lighting those scenes.

"The Borg costumes were torture, from what I was told," says Frakes. "We had our own set of ADs and an entirely separate special effects makeup crew, and the costume department had a certain number of Borg to build and rebuild. Now the Borg had been on the show, but with these Borg we had more time and more moving parts. It was kind of an enhanced thing that really paid off. I look back so fondly on that entire experience. Also, the Borg were one of the great movie villains. They held up!"

Frakes couldn’t be prouder of "First Contact", and he reminds us that most people like it right next to 1982's "Star Trek II: The Wrath of Khan." That's rarefied air indeed!

"We got Cromwell coming off of 'Babe.' So we had Alfre and Alice and Cromwell. They joined our family effortlessly. Because we'd done seven TV seasons, 182 episodes, and a movie already together, we were thick as thieves and still are; may Patrick rest in peace. The three of them joined us as if we’d been dancing with them forever."

"Star Trek: First Contact" is available to stream on Paramount+.

#679. Germany news: Germany holds national day of remembrance

Events were held for "Volkstrauertag," a day commemorating victims of war and oppression. Meanwhile, experts said the country is headed for a budget crisis.

This live blog is now closed. Read on for a roundup of the top stories from and about Germany on the weekend of November 14-15, 2026:

Thank you for reading this weekend's Germany news blog.

We'll bring you more from the heart of Europe on Monday. We wish you a very Schönen Abend!

Austrian President Alexander Van der Bellen has urged Europeans to defend compassion and humanity during Germany's national day of mourning for victims of war and oppression.

Speaking at a ceremony in the Bundestag in Berlin, Van der Bellen warned against becoming desensitized to suffering despite the constant images of war and violence.

"Compassion is not a weakness; it is a human strength; it is the foundation of humanity," he said.

He also addressed the responsibility of later generations for the crimes of the past.

Although people today bore no personal guilt for their ancestors' actions, he said, they were responsible for what they learned from history and how they treated others.

"Let us ensure that our home, Europe, remains a place where people can live in peace, freedom and dignity," he said.

Bundestag President Julia Klöckner also called for the defense of democracy, pointing to Ukrainians risking their lives to protect freedom.

Germany's Volkstrauertag commemorates soldiers and civilians killed in war, as well as victims of Nazi persecution and other forms of oppression.

German police have arrested three suspects after thieves rammed a car into a jewelry store in the Bavarian city of Bayreuth and stole valuables worth around €10,000 ($11,600).

Bavarian Interior Minister Joachim Herrmann said the stolen items included jewelry and silver coins.

The burglars drove a car into the store early in the morning before fleeing in a second vehicle, police said.

Officers spotted the getaway car on the A9 highway and gave chase. The suspects left the highway near Weidensees, abandoned their vehicle beside a wooded area and fled on foot.

Police launched a search involving patrol cars, dogs, drones and a helicopter.

All three suspects were subsequently arrested, with some of the stolen goods recovered.

Prosecutors are expected to decide whether to seek pretrial detention for the suspects.

Detroit Lions receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown played his first NFL American football game in Germany in Munich.

St. Brown made his professional debut in Germany as the Detroit Lions faced the New England Patriots at Munich's Allianz Arena. The 27-year-old grew up in Southern California, and his mother, Miriam, is from Leverkusen. Both his parents were due to watch from the stands.

The NFL player spent childhood summers with his grandparents in the Rhineland.

"This is awesome. A dream come true," St. Brown said before the game. Asked by German broadcaster RTL what he had been looking forward to most, he reeled off a list that included schnitzel, potato dumplings, sauerkraut, currywurst and fries with mayonnaise.

"I'm really excited. I can't wait," he said. "Being in Germany with my teammates and my family — I want to enjoy it and take it all in."

Two people were slightly injured after an unidentified man threw a firework into the entrance of a gay bar in Frankfurt, police said.

The attack took place at the Zum Schwejk bar, a venue popular with the city's gay community, on Saturday evening.

Police said the bar was clearly identifiable as an LGBTQ+ venue because of a rainbow flag displayed outside.

The motive remains unclear, and police have not said whether they suspect a homophobic attack.

Officers are investigating suspected aggravated assault and have appealed for witnesses.

The bar said it was "shocked and stunned" by the incident and apologized to guests who witnessed it. It said it wanted to be a place where everyone felt welcome, respected and safe, and pledged to do everything it could to prevent a repeat.

Andreas Ewald, LGBTQ+ policy spokesperson for the Greens in the Hesse state parliament, condemned the attack and called for those responsible to face the full force of the law.

He also urged the state government to establish a roundtable on LGBTQ+ safety involving community representatives, police and victim support organizations.

The bar's name refers to a Czech soldier in the satirical anti-war novel "The Good Soldier Svejk."

Police in Berlin have filed 28 criminal charges against demonstrators who marched throught the capital on Saturday as part of the Gen Z regelt (Gen Z Takes Charge) movement.

Some 1,200 demonstrators took part in the march, although only 100 had registered for the event under German laws regulating public protests.

The protesters complained about dilapidated schools, the threat of compulsory military service, cuts to university and social funding and other issues.

Police said there had been some clashes with participants.   A police spokeswoman said the criminal charges were filed for riot, assault, resisting officers and violations of explosives regulations.

Three police officers of the 700 deployed to ensure securty were injured during the demonstration.

November 20 is likely to see more large protests in both Germany and Europe, with some 15,000 demonstrators registered for a march in Berlin.

German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier has expressed solidarity with the Jewish community in Germany amid what he described as ever "louder and more aggressive" antisemitic voices.

Speaking at the presentation of the Prize for Understanding and Tolerance awarded by the Jewish Museum in Berlin, Steinmeier said: "For all those to whom our country, its constitution and the values it enshrines mean something, there can be only one answer to such antisemitism: to stand side by side with Jewish people in our country."

Steinmeier said he deplored the frequent vandalism of memorials to Nazi crimes.

"I am profoundly ashamed of that all," he said, saying that anyone who mocked the work of museums and memorial sites or collectively blamed, threatened and attacked Jews "attacks the heart of our republic."

The president also congratulated the prize winners — German journalist and author Düzen Tekkal and British philanthropist Michael Moritz — on their awards.

In a citation, the museum described Tekkal as a champion of human rights who consistently opposed antisemitism and racism while promoting interfaith dialogue, equality in education and opportunities, peace and democracy.

The museum commended Moritz for supporting artistic projects that show Jewish perspectives and strengthen social dialogue.

The Jewish Museum, which is marking its 25th anniversary this year, has been presenting the prize since 2002.

Some 600 sheep have made their way through the southern city of Nuremberg on their way to western winter pasturage, watched by crowds of spectators.

The sheep follow an around 10-km-long (6-mile-long) route that crosses a number of streets and the market square.

The annual event is meant, among other things, to draw attention to the tradition of transhumant, or itinerant, sheep-keeping in the region and the benefits the animals have for landscape conservation.

"With their grazing in summer, sheep create great biodiversity in many important biotopes in the urban region," the city of Nuremberg said ahead of the migration.

Thieves have stolen several valuable items from a jewelry shop in the southern city of Bayreuth after ramming it with a car, police said on Sunday.

They said a black Mercedes carrying three people crashed into the shop in the early hours of Sunday morning.

The burglars then fled the scene in a second Mercedes, this time a gray one, after taking a number of articles.

The getaway car was then spotted by a police patrol on a motorway heading south, with officers setting off in pursuit.

The suspects were then said to have driven off the motorway to a patch of woodland where they abandoned their vehicle and went on by foot.

Police searched for the fugitives with patrol cars, police dogs, drones and a helicopter, a statement said.

Two men were reportedly arrested with a third still on the run. Investigators are looking into whether the detainees were connected with the theft.

Events are taking place around Germany for the Volkstrauertag (people's day of mourning), a day on which armed forces personnel and civilians who died in armed conflicts and victims of violent state oppression are commemorated.

Austrian President Alexander Van der Bellen is to speak in the parliament at the main commemoration ceremony of the German War Graves Commission at midday.

His presence reflects the large number of Austrians who were killed in action in the Second World War while fighting for the German Wehrmacht following the annexation of their country by Nazi Germany in 1938.

German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier, the patron of the commission, will also hold a speech and lay a wreath.

Last year, Steinmeier decreed that the Volkstrauertag should also commemorate people who were persecuted and killed by the Nazis because of their sexual identity, as well as police officers who have lost their lives in the course of duty.

There will also be a remembrance ceremony at the Jewish Cemetery in Berlin for those of the Jewish faith killed in World War I.

In remarks to the DPA news agency ahead of the remembrance day, the speaker of the lower house of German parliament, or Bundestag, Julia Klöckner, called on society to actively defend democracy.

Klöckner said that the Volkstrauertag was a reminder of how destructive tyranny and contempt for human dignity can be.

"Democracy is the antidote here," she said. "But it is not an heirloom. It wastes away when we do not constantly renew its promise of basic rights and freedom."

Guten Morgen from the DW newsroom on the banks of the Rhine in Bonn!

You join us as Germany holds a day of remembrance for the victims of war and oppression and also commemorates members of the police force killed while carrying out their duties.

Read on here for the top stories from and about Germany on Sunday, November 15,

It's 1 a.m. here and time for us to pause our coverage of news from Germany.

We'll be back Sunday morning with more of what's making headlines in Berlin, Bavaria and the rest of the country.

Germany wants to turn its spies into "real secret agents." A sweeping reform could allow them to sabotage threats abroad and use AI to analyze intelligence data.

But why does Germany need these powers now? And how far can its secret services go in a country with a history of strict limits on intelligence operations?

Hundreds of mourners gathered at Munich's Frauenkirche on Saturday to pay their final respects to Hubert Aiwanger, Bavaria's former deputy premier and economy minister, who died unexpectedly at the age of 55.

The ceremony combined a Catholic funeral Mass with a state memorial service, attended by leading political figures, church representatives and members of Bavaria's former royal family.

Bavarian Premier Markus Söder recalled his disbelief when he first heard of Aiwanger's death in a Berlin hotel on November 4. He described his former deputy as someone who had always been full of energy.

Bavarian parliament president Ilse Aigner praised Aiwanger as one of the greatest political talents of his generation, highlighting his role in transforming his party "Freie Wähler" (Free Voters) from a local political movement into a governing party.

Aiwanger's partner, Tanja Schweiger, and their two sons were among those attending the service, which took place eleven days after his death.

German airline group Lufthansa says it was only slightly affected by Friday's temporary suspension of flights to the United States.

Most flights operated as scheduled, although some were canceled or delayed. Lufthansa expects its US flight schedule to return to normal on Saturday but warned that isolated delays could still occur.

Affected passengers are being notified by email, with alternative travel options provided automatically in the event of cancellations.

The disruption was caused by problems with the US air traffic control system. Domestic flights in the US were grounded for around four hours, marking the longest nationwide ground stop since the September 11 attacks in 2001.
